One-page synthesis

Core thesis. Classic MPNs are clonal HSC disorders unified by JAK2-pathway activation but diversified by driver type, mutation order, comutations, inflammation, stem-cell context, and microenvironment. Current treatment largely controls vascular risk and symptoms; the field is shifting toward clone-directed, mutant-selective therapy, especially mutant CALR and JAK2 V617F strategies.

The review’s major conceptual contribution is the linkage of long preclinical clonal latency to a potential early-intervention window. JAK2 V617F can precede diagnosis by decades, while secondary mutations, inflammatory remodeling, fibrosis, and leukemic evolution accumulate later. This supports a future model in which therapy is judged not only by blood counts, spleen volume, or symptoms, but by molecular and stem-cell effects.

Clinical maturity is heterogeneous. Conventional thrombosis prevention, cytoreduction, pegylated interferon, and approved JAK inhibitors have established roles, although the review emphasizes their limited ability to eradicate the malignant clone. Mutant-CALR antibodies, bispecifics, selective JAK2 inhibitors, type II JAK2 inhibitors, epigenetic combinations, and other disease-modifying candidates are promising but many remain preclinical or early phase. The source should therefore inform mechanism, trial interpretation, and future-direction thinking more than independent practice recommendations.

Main limitation: no systematic literature-search method, evidence-grading framework, or formal recommendation process is reported. Apparent treatment efficacy in narrative text and tables spans preclinical models, early data cutoffs, phase 1/2 trials, and ongoing phase 3 studies.

Section-by-section synthesis

Summary and scope

The review frames classic MPNs—essential thrombocythemia (ET), polycythemia vera (PV), and primary myelofibrosis (PMF)—as related clonal HSC diseases unified by aberrant JAK2 signaling. JAK2, CALR, or MPL phenotypic driver mutations are reported in more than 90% of cases; the remainder are termed triple-negative. Shared clinical problems include thrombosis, hemorrhage, secondary myelofibrosis, and transformation to secondary AML.

The article is organized around disease biology, clonal evolution, inflammation, current treatment, and emerging mutant-selective therapy. It is a narrative review: no systematic search strategy, evidence-grading method, or formal recommendation process is reported, so the source is best used as an expert synthesis rather than as a stand-alone guideline.

Activation of JAK2 and cytokine-receptor signaling

JAK2 V617F constitutively activates MPL, EPOR, and probably G-CSF receptor signaling through STAT, RAS–MAPK, and PI3K pathways. Mutant CALR acquires a new C terminus, binds MPL, and drives MPL dimerization and JAK2–STAT activation; mutant CALR secretion also contributes to ER stress and the unfolded-protein response. MPL W515 and S505N mutations favor ligand-independent receptor dimerization and activation.

Figure 1 is mechanistically load-bearing because it distinguishes the abnormal receptor conformations and the signaling consequences of JAK2 V617F, mutant CALR, and mutant MPL. The review emphasizes that mutant CALR and MPL are largely restricted to megakaryocytic phenotypes (ET/PMF), whereas JAK2 V617F spans ET, PV, and PMF.

Driver mutations in HSCs and clonal phylogeny

All three canonical driver classes arise in multipotent HSCs, but amplification is predominantly myeloid. JAK2 V617F is described as providing modest HSC advantage with strong lineage-differentiation effects; CALR-mutant HSCs preferentially amplify the megakaryocytic lineage. MPL and thrombopoietin are central to the clonal fitness of JAK2 V617F HSCs, making MPL itself a potential cross-driver therapeutic target.

Phylogenetic studies summarized by the review indicate that JAK2 V617F can arise decades before clinical disease, even in utero, with highly variable clone growth. CALR is generally acquired later but may confer higher fitness. This long preclinical interval becomes a central premise for the authors’ early-intervention argument.

Somatic clonal-fitness and germline factors

About half of cases are described as carrying only the MPN driver mutation; the rest harbor additional lesions in epigenetic, spliceosomal, signaling, or transcriptional genes. PMF generally carries a higher burden of these mutations than ET or PV, and several mutations—including SRSF2, U2AF1-Q157, ASXL1, IDH1/2, and EZH2—are associated with adverse prognosis. Multihit TP53 is linked to therapy-resistant leukemia, whereas the meaning of single TP53 lesions is less certain.

Familial clustering and common risk alleles such as the 46/1 haplotype support inherited predisposition, while rarer variants involving EPOR, RBBP6, SH2B3, and 14q32 duplication are more penetrant but mechanistically less settled. Figure 2 shows the increasing frequency of adverse comutations and cytogenetic lesions along progression toward myelofibrosis and AML.

Inflammation, fibrosis, and thrombosis

The review treats inflammation as a disease engine rather than a by-product. JAK2-driven STAT3 and NF-κB activity in clonal and nonclonal cells contributes to constitutional symptoms. IL-1β and TNF-α remodel the HSC niche; megakaryocyte-derived TGF-β1, IL-1β, and IL-8 promote mesenchymal conversion toward fibrotic cell types; senescent neutrophils and monocyte-derived fibrocytes further reinforce fibrosis.

Inflammation also links to thrombosis through endothelial, platelet, leukocyte, NET, and coagulation activation. Because inflammation can promote both clonal selection and vascular complications, the authors identify anti-inflammatory targeting as a plausible therapeutic axis, though the review does not provide a graded clinical recommendation for a specific anti-inflammatory strategy.

Transformation to secondary AML

Secondary AML is presented as the most severe evolutionary endpoint, with a median overall survival of only 3–5 months. The review reports increasing cumulative AML risk across ET, PV, and especially PMF. Post-MPN AML differs molecularly from de novo AML: classic FLT3/NPM1/CEBPA lesions are less common, whereas epigenetic, spliceosomal, transcriptional, TP53, and cytogenetic abnormalities are prominent.

The leukemic clone may retain or lose the original MPN driver. Loss of JAK2 V617F can reflect leukemic evolution from a preexisting clonal-hematopoiesis ancestor or an independent competing clone. Multihit TP53 is particularly adverse. Allogeneic HSC transplantation is described as the only curative option, but feasibility and success are limited.

Current treatment

Conventional management targets thrombosis, symptoms, and excessive blood counts with phlebotomy, low-dose aspirin, hydroxyurea, pegylated interferon, and JAK inhibitors according to disease and risk. Pegylated interferon can produce hematologic and molecular responses in ET/PV and is attractive for younger patients and pregnancy; deeper JAK2 V617F allele-burden reduction generally requires prolonged treatment.

Approved type I JAK2 inhibitors—ruxolitinib, fedratinib, momelotinib, and pacritinib—do not selectively inhibit mutant JAK2. They mainly improve inflammation-driven symptoms and splenomegaly and can reduce thrombosis, but disease-modifying effects are limited and cytopenias remain important. Momelotinib is differentiated by anemia benefit through combined JAK1/JAK2 and ACVR1 activity.

Toward disease-modifying treatment

The most mature mutant-selective program described is mutant CALR targeting. INCA033989, a monoclonal antibody, and JNJ-88549968, a mutant-CALR/CD3 bispecific, are designed to exploit a neoantigen absent from normal cells. Early INCA033989 data summarized by the review show high hematologic/molecular response rates in CALR-mutated ET, but these data are early phase and should not be treated as established comparative efficacy. Vaccine strategies have been less convincing so far.

For JAK2 V617F, approaches include enhanced interferon combinations, selective allosteric JH2 inhibitors such as INCB160058, type II JAK2 inhibitors such as AJ1-11095, and combinations targeting epigenetic, nuclear-export, MDM2, BCL-xL, or telomerase biology. Tables 1 and 2 mix preclinical, phase 1/2, and ongoing phase 3 evidence; maturity therefore varies substantially by agent.

Conclusions

The authors’ unifying thesis is that MPN biology is moving from nonspecific control of counts, symptoms, and inflammation toward mutant-selective, clone-directed therapy. The long interval between driver acquisition and overt disease creates a theoretical opportunity to intervene before secondary mutations, fibrosis, thrombosis, or leukemic evolution accumulate.

The main unresolved issues are when a clone remains driver-dependent, how comutations alter treatment response, whether selective therapy could reveal competing clones, and what toxicity is acceptable for early intervention. The review concludes that early treatment may be essential for true clonal modification, but this remains a forward-looking proposition rather than an evidence-graded standard of care.

Figure 1 — Main structures and oncogenic signaling of JAK2 V617F, mutant CALR, and MPL

Load-bearing relationship: mutant CALR and MPL activate MPL–JAK2–STAT signaling, whereas JAK2 V617F can signal through MPL, EPOR, and G-CSF receptor. The figure explains why phenotypes and potential targets differ by driver.

Figure 2 — Drivers and associated comutations across disease progression

The visual maps driver/comutation and cytogenetic patterns across ET, PV, myelofibrosis, and secondary AML. It supports the review’s claim that adverse comutations and chromosomal lesions accumulate with advanced disease.

The algorithm is adapted from multiple consensus guidelines and prognostic systems and is explicitly noted by the authors as not universally accepted; authorization and country-specific practice can differ.

Evaluation and appraisal

Verdict: Read first. Best used as a 2026 MPN landscape review connecting driver biology, clonal evolution, inflammation, current treatment, and mutant-selective therapies. Do not use as the sole authority for patient-specific treatment selection.
9/10
Relevance

Very high for MPN pathobiology and modern treatment direction.

Evidence basis: Current, disease-wide synthesis spanning biology, complications, standard therapy, and emerging agents.
Principal limiting factor: Not a narrow clinical decision guideline.
What changes the score: Would fall if the task were unrelated to MPN/hematology; would rise to 10 for an MPN-focused research or teaching task.
8/10
Novelty

Integrates the long-latency model with clone-directed therapeutic development.

Evidence basis: Emphasizes mutant CALR and selective JAK2 programs and early-intervention framing.
Principal limiting factor: Many mechanistic components and standard treatments predate 2026.
What changes the score: Would rise with demonstrated clinical validation of the emerging selective therapies.
4/10
Method strength

Narrative expert review without a reported systematic search or evidence-grading framework.

Evidence basis: Broad citation base and specialist synthesis.
Principal limiting factor: No reproducible search, selection, risk-of-bias, or certainty method.
What changes the score: Would rise with prespecified search methods and evidence grading.
6/10
Evidence strength

Claims are supported by a mix of established studies, trials, and preclinical work, but maturity varies widely.

Evidence basis: Includes established clinical programs and explicit trial tables.
Principal limiting factor: Early-phase, preclinical, and ongoing trials are discussed alongside established care.
What changes the score: Would rise with mature randomized outcomes and consistent certainty assessment.
7/10
External validity

The disease-wide concepts are broadly applicable across classic MPNs.

Evidence basis: Covers ET, PV, PMF, secondary AML, risk scores, and multinational guideline-derived algorithms.
Principal limiting factor: Drug authorization and treatment algorithms vary by country; early therapies have narrow trial populations.
What changes the score: Would rise with cross-system implementation data and mature approvals.
8/10
Implementation value

Strong for teaching, trial interpretation, and identifying therapeutic directions.

Evidence basis: Provides mechanisms, algorithms, risk tools, trial IDs, and treatment-development tables.
Principal limiting factor: Should not be used alone to set patient-level therapy because it is not a formal guideline/label.
What changes the score: Would rise with formal recommendations, dosing/monitoring detail, and jurisdiction-specific approval status.

Main strengths

Current synthesis; coherent mechanistic model; strong integration of clonal phylogeny and inflammation; clear separation of established treatment from emerging mutant-selective strategies; trial identifiers and supplementary risk-score tables improve reuse.

Main limitations

No systematic-review methods or evidence-certainty grading; heterogeneous evidence maturity; some early clinical results are reported only at preliminary data cutoffs; practice algorithms are adapted from multiple guidelines and explicitly not universally accepted.

Clinical-use boundary: a narrative review can accurately summarize current evidence while still being insufficient for final dosing, contraindication, monitoring, approval, or guideline decisions. Those require direct consultation of current guidelines, regulatory labeling, and local policy.

Confidence in appraisal: high for source characterization and internal content; moderate for practice translation because no external recency verification was requested or performed.

Practice and implementation takeaways

Use now
Use the review to structure MPN teaching, interpret why ET/PV/PMF diverge despite shared JAK2-pathway biology, and identify the logic behind interferon, JAK inhibition, risk stratification, and transplant referral.
Watch closely
Mutant-CALR antibodies/bispecifics, selective JAK2 V617F inhibitors, type II JAK2 inhibitors, and combination strategies that may move endpoints from symptom control toward molecular/clonal modification.
Do not overclaim
Early phase response percentages, preclinical clone eradication, and ongoing phase 3 programs should not be presented as established comparative efficacy or routine standard of care.
Research implication
Future trials should pair clinical endpoints with molecular and single-cell measurements that determine whether disease-initiating HSCs and adverse subclones are actually reduced.
